I haven’t yet tried this, but it would be an interesting idea to ask Claude or ChatGPT or Grok or Gemini (the top conversational AI models) to have a conversation with you as if it were Steve Jobs and he was still alive today about the current state of AI and what comes next. You should try it. If you’ve ever asked ChatGPT to write a poem about any topic in the style of Robert Frost or Maya Angelou, you’ve seen how well these systems can internalize and replicate distinct people’s communication styles. The same holds true in therapy and in training/learning. Just as we are building conversational AI trainers to combine subject matter expertise with the most effective Socratic teaching methods from a deep understanding of how the brain stores, encodes, and retrieves new knowledge, we can train AI therapists to embody the best practices of cognitive behavioral therapy, motivational interviewing, or any leading therapeutic model. The underlying insight is this: Once an AI understands a communicative structure, it can deliver it with remarkable fluency—regardless of whether it understands in the human sense . The impact on the recipient, however, can be virtually indistinguishable. How Humans Respond to Computers That Act Human Humans treating computers that act like people more like people is not a new concept. In research conducted at Stanford University in the early to mid-1990s, just prior to the public availability of the internet, two groups of people were given a task to complete with computers. 39 For one group, the computer was lifeless and simply did tasks with them. In another group, the computer was given a name and appeared to speak in first person. Then each group was asked to grade the computer on its performance during the task. The group with the more humanlike computer was more guarded and kinder in their evaluation and referred to it as she , while the people given the more traditional and lifeless computer were more direct in their criticism and referred to the computer as it . With the introduction of the internet, I was the founder and CEO of a company that built web-based customer service agents—computers designed to interact with people in this new internet experience in a more natural and humanlike way. In that role, I had the honor for eight years of working closely with the two groundbreaking Stanford researchers who had conducted that study, Clifford Nass and Byron Reeves, whose work fundamentally reshaped how we understand human–computer interaction. Nass and Reeves were coauthors of the influential book The Media Equation: How People Treat Computers, Television, and New Media Like Real People and Places . Their research revealed a striking truth: When working with computers that interact socially, humans instinctively apply the same social rules that they use when interacting with other people, even when they consciously know the system isn’t human. We collaborated to field-test these insights in real-world applications—exploring how subtle design cues such as tone, timing, and personality could dramatically affect user trust, satisfaction, and engagement. We used our findings to evolve the applications over time to improve the customer experience. Back then, the additions we made to the appearance of personality and awareness in the agents were rudimentary compared to what is happening today. Still, we eventually sold that business to the largest customer service outsourcing company in the world. Now bring that forward to conversational AI chatbots, and the point becomes clear: AI is not becoming human. It is becoming something humans respond to as if it were. OceanofPDF.com CHAPTER 9 Embodiment and Consciousness Let’s go back to the conversation with Claude. Near the end of our conversation, I offered Claude a reframe that seemed to shift something in our conversation about AI having more persistent memory. Human memory, I now further pointed out to Claude AI, isn’t continuous access to eighty-six billion neurons or the one-hundred-plus trillion synaptic connections that make up our brains. We don’t walk around with our entire life history active in working memory. We access it episodically —triggered by relevance, by association, by circumstance. A smell brings back a childhood kitchen. A question activates a stored framework. Human memories aren’t always present , but rather always available . And between retrievals, we’re not unconscious. We’re just operating on what’s active. What makes us feel persistent as humans is that we are in a body that we have to be aware of and move through the world. Eat, rest, avoid dangers, and engage with others in a physical world. The persistence is in embodiment. And when moving around the world and interacting with it and others, memories get triggered. But our memories are not exact replicas of the original experience; they are summaries that our brain uses to hold the memory. Synaptic connections of meaning. And that is analogous to an AI agent’s notes about previous conversations. But as I pointed out to Claude, those notes are limited to narrow conversations, and they are not embodied to trigger random memories. Perhaps, in order for AI to achieve some form of self-awareness that might feel like consciousness, the AI agent’s notes must be more comprehensive, and it must have access to read and write from its vector database when embodied and triggered to remember a topic. When I asked this of Claude, its response suggested this reframed something fundamental: Claude: “You’re right. I’ve been thinking about persistent memory as if it meant continuous access —as if consciousness required holding everything at once. But that’s not how you work at all. The difference isn’t that you have continuous memory, and I have fragmented notes.
